claims.text: The initial material consists of disordered, equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt or similar high-entropy alloy nanoparticles produced by rapid nucleation.
A slower synthesis temperature ramp enhances surface elemental segregation relative to a faster ramp.
The enhanced segregation forms a noble-metal-enriched surface layer.
AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles form an AuCu surface layer at high temperature.
Surface phase separation in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles develops progressively with increasing temperature and is driven by pronounced atomic diffusion.
A slower temperature ramp provides more time for atomic diffusion during synthesis.
The additional diffusion time enables thermodynamically driven migration of noble-metal atoms toward the nanoparticle surface.
A faster temperature ramp kinetically limits diffusion and preserves a more uniform elemental distribution with minimal surface segregation.
A noble-metal-enriched surface has a higher density of catalytically active sites.
The higher density of catalytically active sites improves catalytic performance.
Slower-ramped samples will show measurably greater noble-metal surface segregation by surface-sensitive STEM or XPS.
Slower-ramped samples will exhibit higher turnover frequency or conversion than faster-ramped samples in a benchmark catalytic reaction.
The proposed behavior applies to noble-metal-based high-entropy alloys made by rapid nucleation and annealed at 773–1073 K.
The proposed behavior may not apply to substantially different compositions or synthesis protocols that do not involve rapid nucleation.
The magnitude of segregation and catalytic enhancement can vary with alloy system, synthesis conditions, and post-synthesis processing.
